comment_text.value:
> “Formally verified” does not mean “bug-free.”

Is formal verification the path forward? Meh... I dont think so. Does it have applications in some areas: yes. But this is just more robust "unit testing".

Anthropic keeps trying to convince you that "one agent" will do the job. It does so with the statement "We built 36 small verification tasks from real OSS-Fuzz code. Opus 5.5 proves half of them with about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5. We expect this trend to continue as models are trained on long verification tasks."

But this is not the path forward. Robust E2E, durable (can your app go from python to rust with out loosing tests) Simulation/Emulation tests are the way. This is an "in bulk" and "brute force" activity. Go look at TigerBeetle for an example of this in practice. Go look at how oxide is doing testing.

Can a swarm of cheaper agents write these tests more effectively that Anthropics premium products. I assure you that it can.

If you look at OAI's actions (hugging face hack) and anthropic own publication on its version control AI is not a best of breed solution its a brute force hammer at it till you get what you need solution.

story_title.value: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale

comment_text.value:
I led a team of a dozen developers to write software required to make the movie.

We were working with very early (beta) versions of Maya running on Silicon Graphics workstations. My team developed software for simulating hair and clothing, deformation and surface refinement tools, and anything else required to generate "photorealistic" humans.

As most things with my career, there were fortuitous coincidences. I was working on early hair and cloth simulation at a startup in Montreal and someone I briefly crossed paths with ended up at Square USA and recommended me to the company. The industry was very different 30 years ago: there were very few people working on things such as CG hair and cloth.

I am now teaching computer graphics at the University of Hawaii. Passing on what I know to the new generation.

It remains to be seen what the impact of AI will be on the industry and art form. I am currently creating a new course on AI and animation to be taught next year.

story_title.value: AMA – "Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within", milestone in CGI, is 25 years old

comment_text.value:
> I don't think there are actually that many domains where you can't simulate them with enough knowledge and compute.

The problem is that you have to simulate them accurately enough and fast enough. A perfect simulation of physics will necessarily be orders of magnitude slower than physics. To accelerate it, you need to figure out which parts can be cut or approximated without derailing the model, and just that part will require a lot of back and forth with reality.

Success isn't guaranteed either. If a physical system does whatever it does optimally enough, fast simulation is just physically impossible. Furthermore, even simple chaotic systems require unrealistic precision in the initial parameters to be useful. Natural entities are fairly chaotic and also pretty darn efficient at what they do, so it's plausible that even the best possible simulation of a middle manager is a slower bottleneck than a real middle manager.

story_title.value: The Decoherence Trap

comment_text.value:
> Indirect Realism

> we don’t perceive the world per se; our brains instantiate a world-simulation.

Sensory perception described in varying linguistic registers don't really differ at all. It's just a matter of semantic similarity, which depends on the audience ability to refit and reinterpret terms and concepts "down or upwards, left or right", in both, actual and Yankovich-Seuss terms ... so I can't agree with "indirect realism".

Focal attention, peripheral attention, sensory latency and processing speeds, amount of things perceived via all senses in the various mind/brain states and amount of things understood via progressive, cumulative and recursive cognitive processing based on cultural, psycho-social past and contiguously or non-contiguously ( coma & stuff ) resulting experiences and the intensity/relevance of these experiences effects/impact on the self and desires vary so brutally that it's impossible to simulate the world that we perceive in the same freaking way in pretty much every single brain.

The only thing imaginable to me is something similar to the whole universal grammar in baby brains theory, which I agree with but somewhat clumsily extend slightly deeper to the electrochemical domain of micro-voltages in intra- and extra-cellular osmotic environments. I don't think brains instantiate a world-simulation.

The only thing (within the given frame of reference) brains instantiate is a screen to watch reality (directly) on. Including that cool feature where you can record stuff and save it on cerebral/neural VHS tapes that degrade over time.

story_title.value: My Working Model of Consciousness

comment_text.value:
Hello HN! Zooki World is a small low-poly zoo that runs in your browser, and is now also available on mobile. You can walk around with other visitors and see the same animals as they do in real time. What makes Zooki World unique is that there is no simulation server. All animal behaviors are deterministic; each two-minute block is used to calculate movement based on an animal's ID, the version of their enclosure, and the current time block.

Therefore, each browser will independently reproduce the exact same movements and pathing. The only role of the server is to synchronize time and send player positions. You can also interact with the animals or purchase treats for them. When you feed an animal, all other visitors will see it happen at the same time. The animals were created using SDF (signed distance field) sculpting instead of traditional blender models. I wrote the simulation, path finding, and server code myself. Claude Code was very helpful, however, I did personally review and refine all of the code. The monetization model is inspired by the "Million Dollar Homepage" where you can "adopt" any enclosure for $1 until someone else outbids you by at least 10%. So far, the numbers are modest: 183 visits since October 9th with one enclosure adopted — by another project of mine. You can view the public statistics here: https://zooki.world/stats I would love to get your feedback: How does it run on your device (GPU, browser, FPS)?

How do the animals look from a standard camera angle?

comment_text.value:
The way this is done in every domain where the real is a bottle neck is with simulation. So the actual argument is: What domains do we think are not practical to simulate even with extreme intelligence making the simulation and the ability to bring immense amounts of computing power to bear while running.

I don't think there are actually that many domains where you can't simulate them with enough knowledge and compute. So then the bottleneck becomes your ability to sample the world and refine your models. For some domains you can have the models run against each other in your sim which greatly reduces the need for real world feedback (see AlphaZero for example).

So in the case of human persuasion, like asking a boss for a raise, the model could of failed many times a second while trying to persuade a simulation of a typical middle manager with the same parameters as your boss.

For some domains you can have the models run against each other in your sim which greatly reduces the need for real world feedback (see AlphaZero for example).

So in the case of human persuasion, like asking a boss for a raise, the model could of failed many times a second while trying to persuade a simulation of a typical middle manager with the same parameters as your boss.

comment_text.value:
My bet is on one of

- A sequence number being accidentally used as the private key or

- The private key being generated securely but then accidentally truncated to 8 bits (e.g. writing a single char into a zeroed buffer when you should've memcpy'd from a char*).

The sequence number idea is supported by the fact that two of the G3B private keys are consecutive numbers. I ran a quick Monte Carlo simulation and if I got it right, sampling 8 keys from [0,255] uniformly at random (as in the truncation scenario), you'd expect them to contain 2 consecutive numbers only about 18% of the time.

comment_text.value:
This points back to a more general problem. I love to haul out the quote "All models are wrong, but some models are useful", and it's actually attributed to a statistician talking about statistical models. The quote was written well before AI, from a mathematician working in a time even before computer science dug into data science/eng.

As presented the Decoherence Trap is AI related, but as someone with a background in physical simulation and modeling, and applying math models & system controls algorithms, software in general has always had a connection-to-reality issue. It's always been able to go faster in building models faster than reality can be checked. People are always eager for the results and to take action on them, when the long run limiting factor is often, can I observe enough real data signal to make a good decision by any set of optimizing model rules. It's often harder and slower to collect real-world data, ideas, and samples than it is to rapidly process it. With AI, I think we can even more quickly build models (not in an llm sense, but in a operational sense) that give beautiful, precise results which may or may not be useful in a connected-to-reality way.

If the model operates on bad data, then the risk is always the temptation of having a precise-looking technical answer to apply. The practices need to be updated, but I think the mindset of systems engineering validation & verification, and software QA are going to be very needed going forward.

There is actually a related issue, in that I don't think we want an overly coherent of set of models running through our economy - it's a strong risk of central planning failings vs competitive/experimental markets, but that's a tangential discussion.

story_title.value: The Decoherence Trap

comment_text.value:
Apologies for opening the discussion with a half related topic, since I haven't finished the article yet, but... Damn, that is one beautiful website.

Edit: Back after reading. I think I have a point about the simulation section. It compares the difference in decoherence introduced in the system by clankers and human devs as if those were different groups.

I suspect if we consider AI a human performance multiplier, we explain easily how supercharging a dysfunctional process just makes it go sideways faster. There are organizational experiments to try there.

For example, what if you only supercharge a section of the company tasked with maintaining coherence?

A common organizational problem is that the people who know and care about the system itself are outnumbered by the rest (juniors, people new to the system, managers rushing jobs, people who want to mark things as done ASAP tactically, etc). This imbalance will multiply when code is mass produced and reviews are dismissed. We're all seeing the senior burnout and cynical YOLOing occurring everywhere.

AI offers a way to rebalance this dynamic, though. You can effectively add multipliers to arbitrary human workers, and get a system that tends to low complexity by design.

You don't have to renounce to speed either. The junior dev will be faster not by being AI-enabled, but by working in an adaptable, understandable system.

story_title.value: The Decoherence Trap

comment_text.value:
So--first thing's first. Scientists know Dark Matter is not complete. Consider the progress we've made from the Copernican model of the solar system, to the Kepler model, to Newtonian gravity, to Einstein's theory of gravity. Right now, our understanding of Dark Matter is at the Kepler stage. We know what it's doing. We do not know why it is doing it.

But we have plenty of observations to lead us to what dark might be and what it definitely isn't.

Any theory of dark matter needs to explain all of the following:

1. The Virial Theorem, galaxy clusters, and the speeds of galaxies in clusters. (both MOND and CDM both do a good job of explaining this)

2. Galactic rotation curves. (MOND and CDM both do a good job of explaining this)

3. Accoustic Baryon Oscillations. (ABO) Immediately after the big bang, everything was ludicrously hot. The most powerful force in the universe was the wash of gamma rays everywhere. These gamma rays carried electrons around. The electric fields of the electrons carried the protons around. (the light dominated phase) As the universe cooled, this flipped; the protons were carried around by momentum, which brought the electrons with them, which mediated the light. (the matter dominated phase, where we are today) During the light dominated phase, sound waves pulsed through the universe, causing dense regions and underdense regions. When the universe flipped from being light dominated to matter dominated, these regions were frozen in time, and we can see them directly in the CMB. (cosmic microwave background) We can analyze the properties of these pressure waves to determine what the properties of the matter and light in the universe were. These waves demand some sort of dark matter. CDM explains these observations, MOND does not.

4. The Bullet Cluster. The Bullet Cluster is a collision of two galaxy clusters. We can measure gravitation lensing and light to determine where the dark matter is and where the regular matter is. The bullet cluster demonstrates that these two properties are not the same. There is matter which has gravity and gravitational lensing, but that we can't see. CDM explains these observations, MOND does not.

5. Ultra diffuse galaxies with very little dark matter. Not all galaxies have galactic rotation curves which require some extra sauce to explain the movement of their stars. Some galaxies are explained perfectly by the matter that we can see in them. So we need dark matter for most galaxies, but some galaxies need to be dark matter free. These galaxies falsify MOND.

6. Leading spiral arms in barred spiral galaxies. The large majority of barred spiral galaxies have their arms trailing from their bars, but a very small number of them have arms which lead in front of the bars. Computer simulations show this happens naturally with CDM, but MOND or dark matter free spiral galaxies don't have a mechanism to cause this to happen.

7. Gravitational waves travel at the speed of light. Most MOND formulations predict gravitational waves travel slower than c; all of those formulations are wrong.

There is a genuinely absurd amount of time, effort, and money that has gone into explaining dark matter. It is not a band aid, we haven't just added 1 to moved on. Everybody is pouring over every step of the algorithm trying to figure out why it's giving us the wrong answer. CDM is the leading hypothesis right now, because it explains all of the observations, and is not falsified by any of the observations. MACHO is/was another theory; it has gone out of fashion because it does not explain all of the observations and makes predictions we do not observe when we check for them. MOND is out of fashion because it is falsified by the data. MOND is still in fashion among a particular brand of people who just want to have their names in the history books; if someone did prove MOND, the history books would all have lists that go "Ptolemy, Copernicus, Kepler, Newton, Einstein, <your name here>."

But for Pete's sake it's not as if people have their fingers in their ears.

explanation of acronyms/terms:

1. Dark Matter. Dark Matter is the observation that the universe acts as if there's a lot more matter in it other than the stuff we can see. Basically no one says that Dark Matter isn't real; that would imply that the observations are wrong.

2. MOND. Modified Newtonian Gravity. MOND is a family of models which aim to explain the dark matter observation. Instead of using F=Gm1m2/r^2 to determine the force of gravity, we have better math, that gives a different equation, that accurately explains Dark Matter. When you say "physicists discover a much more logical explanation" that's what you're talking about.

3. CDM. Cold Dark Matter. CDM is a family of models which aim to explain the dark matter observation. CDM implies that Dark Matter is explained by particles. CDM implies there is some sort of particle of family of particles which interact with normal matter via gravity as normal, via the electromagnetic or strong nuclear force not at all, or via the weak nuclear force super weakly or not at all. CDM interacts with other CDM particles via gravity as normal, but only weakly via either the weak nuclear force or some other as-yet undiscovered force. People often use the terms Dark Matter (referring to the observation) and Cold Dark Matter interchangeably.

4. CMB. Cosmic Microwave Background radiation. After the Big Bang, the universe was opaque. Light would be absorbed by the stuff in the universe and then re-emitted. During recombination, the universe became transparent. The last moment of the various bits and parts of the universe switching from being opaque to transparent has the entire universe glowing in microwaves. This moment is captured in a snapshot, known as the cosmic microwave background. As we understand the CMB better, we learn a lot--a lot a lot--about the early universe.

story_title.value: Triplet of 'ghostly' galaxies hints at what dark matter is and isn't

comment_text.value:
I haven't tried the game, but this is slightly hilarious and awesome.

I've often wondered about this kind of thing. When I go to an airport, it seems strange to me that each one is different with some of them having elaborate train systems, or multiple runways.

The engineer in me says "surely there is an optimal solution, so why are they all so different?". Is there a simulator?

Sim City was a fantastic simulation from the stand point of a game, but I'm curious; if you build a city simulator and let it grow organically (game of life style) can you put in sufficient regulation/parameters that get you to where we are today?

And if so, is there a simulation that shows us a way to get us to a better tomorrow?
